title: Fast Accurate Quantum Monte Carlo without Metropolis Adjustment
topic: Probabilistic Methods->Monte Carlo and Sampling Methods
claim: The faster unadjusted sampler gains efficiency across the whole domain while its asymptotic bias stays small and can be estimated without ground truth.
layout: 4 heatmap panels in a row, left-to-right, shared k-space axes, colorbars
description: A single row of four square heatmaps over the same momentum-space axes (k_x horizontal, k_y vertical). The first shows the fermion occupation n(k) in a red-white-blue diverging colormap. Red lobes sit at the top and bottom and blue lobes at the left and right, around a white central disk. The second panel is titled 'Efficiency Ratio: uMCLMC / aHMC'. It is a noisy red-dominated pixel grid on a log colorbar from 10^0 to above 10^1, so the new method is mostly several times more efficient. The third and fourth panels show asymptotic bias b_a and the ground-truth-free estimate b_ε in viridis. Both have the same ring of brighter patches near the lobe regions, and the two look nearly identical. A shared colorbar on the far right runs from 0 to about 0.35. The eye goes first to the colorful n(k) panel, then the red efficiency noise.
caption: Analysis of efficiency and asymptotic bias for a fermionic observable. Column 1: Fermion occupation n(k) at L = 64, Nτ = 40, λ = 2.65. Column 2: Corresponding improvement of uMCLMC over aHMC, as measured by ESSn (section 5). Column 3: Asymptotic bias ba, measured by comparison to a long aHMC ground truth run, is controlled. Column 4: Estimate of asymptotic bias without ground truth samples, bϵ; ba is generally no greater than twice bϵ, so that bias in unadjusted methods may be diagnosed safely without reference to an adjusted method.
abstract: In quantum systems, physical quantities of interest can be expressed as expectation values of a probability distribution, which allows their estimation by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. This approach, an instance of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), plays a central role in obtaining predictions of system properties relevant to condensed matter and high energy physics. The use of Hamiltonian dynamics to design a Markov kernel, known as Hybrid or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), is widespread in quantum applications. In this context, it is standard to use an HMC kernel that is ``adjusted'' with the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) criterion, so that estimates of expectations converge to their true value in the limit of infinite sample size. However, recent work in computational statistics suggests that an \emph{unadjusted} HMC kernel can be significantly more efficient, while safely maintaining an asymptotic bias which is small relative to the error arising from the variance of the finite sample size. We adapt this approach to the QMC setting, focusing on a challenging and high-dimensional \emph{spin-fermion} model of a quantum phase transition. We find that unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in terms of effective sample size per gradient call, while retaining accurate results.
